ketch_nodepy.HypothesizedGapReason: Likely occasional maintenance of an established research tool: all ten pre-gap messages concern documentation, ending with the README badge change [147d0828](https://github.com/ketch/nodepy/commit/147d0828c75dd52c54be0a8271846103c2a15409). The exact cause of the 11-month pause is not documented in the inspected evidence.
ketch_nodepy.HasRecovered: Partly: two commits on September 4, 2024; sustained recovery is not established.
ketch_nodepy.WhyRecovered: The visible trigger was a correction to SSP(5,4) coefficients ([1ea45f78](https://github.com/ketch/nodepy/commit/1ea45f786c297fbc1f73e8f4e531bf0d795dea6f)), followed by a README-related merge. Only these two post-gap records are available.
ketch_nodepy.WhoRecovered: David Ketcheson authored both post-gap commits and already appears before the gap, including [147d0828](https://github.com/ketch/nodepy/commit/147d0828c75dd52c54be0a8271846103c2a15409); no new raw author identity appears in this sample.
ketch_nodepy.Notes: NodePy has an 11-month gap after a run of documentation maintenance. David Ketcheson later corrected numerical coefficients, but only two post-gap commits are available. This supports a small return to maintenance, while the exact reason for the pause remains unclear.
ketch_nodepy.reflection: The 11-month gap follows documentation edits rather than a major feature change. The final pre-gap commit, [147d0828](https://github.com/ketch/nodepy/commit/147d0828c75dd52c54be0a8271846103c2a15409), changes a README badge, while the first return, [1ea45f78](https://github.com/ketch/nodepy/commit/1ea45f786c297fbc1f73e8f4e531bf0d795dea6f), improves numerical coefficients. That looks like occasional maintenance of a research tool, but it does not explain the maintainer's availability or priorities. The README at the boundary still invited contributions, and the inspected issue/PR searches did not identify an announcement explaining the pause. With only two later commits in Part 1, it would be too strong to call this a sustained recovery.

mouseland_suite2p.HypothesizedGapReason: A short maintenance lull is plausible because the only empty month is November 2024 and nearby commits repair GUI and input-handling problems. Issues #1144 and #1149 were open before the gap; they show pending work, but do not establish why committing paused.
mouseland_suite2p.HasRecovered: Yes: commits resume in December 2024 and Part 1 contains 347 dated commits after the gap.
mouseland_suite2p.WhyRecovered: The return addressed registration-metric issue #1144 ([7bb28c69](https://github.com/MouseLand/suite2p/commit/7bb28c69e6c020c3c7ac963968563620045167af)) and HDF5-input issue #1149 ([2c406958](https://github.com/MouseLand/suite2p/commit/2c4069586f5c84439124a3586a45488841417ef9)). Chris Ki confirmed those fixes in the linked issue discussions.
mouseland_suite2p.WhoRecovered: Chris Ki wrote nine of the first ten post-gap commits using two existing email identities; calebshibu authored the other merge. All three raw author strings already occur in the full pre-gap history, although none is in the last-ten pre-gap sample.
mouseland_suite2p.Notes: Suite2p has one empty month, followed by fixes to previously reported bugs. Chris Ki drives the immediate return, with the same raw identities already present earlier in the project. The issue discussions explain the work that resumed, but not why committing paused during November.
mouseland_suite2p.reflection: The November 2024 gap is short, so it is hard to interpret it as abandonment. Most of the pre-gap sample fixes GUI, logging, and file-path problems. The first post-gap change ([7bb28c69](https://github.com/MouseLand/suite2p/commit/7bb28c69e6c020c3c7ac963968563620045167af)) fixes registration metrics, and another ([2c406958](https://github.com/MouseLand/suite2p/commit/2c4069586f5c84439124a3586a45488841417ef9)) handles lists of HDF5 files. [Issue #1144](https://github.com/MouseLand/suite2p/issues/1144) and [issue #1149](https://github.com/MouseLand/suite2p/issues/1149) were reported before the gap and closed when Chris Ki described the fixes in December. A temporary maintenance lull is a reasonable hypothesis; the discussions do not identify a staffing or funding cause. The 347 later dated records provide stronger evidence of continued work than the first ten commits alone.

esri_geoportal-server.HypothesizedGapReason: The repository is the retired Geoportal Server v1 archive. The README before and after the gap directs users to successor repositories and states that updates are not planned ([cd9bdd2f](https://github.com/Esri/geoportal-server/commit/cd9bdd2fbd4ffa07e3d7b50813c9ff462fc6af2b)); this directly supports reduced development.
esri_geoportal-server.HasRecovered: No sustained development recovery: only two documentation commits follow the gap in Part 1.
esri_geoportal-server.WhyRecovered: Limited repository maintenance resumed: [cd9bdd2f](https://github.com/Esri/geoportal-server/commit/cd9bdd2fbd4ffa07e3d7b50813c9ff462fc6af2b) revises retirement and successor information, and [3014a9ce](https://github.com/Esri/geoportal-server/commit/3014a9ce2120bd33ddde44bd4dae139775ec3785) adjusts the project website. Neither inspected diff adds application functionality.
esri_geoportal-server.WhoRecovered: Marten Hogeweg, using the existing Marten <mhogeweg@esri.com> identity, authored both post-gap documentation commits. This identity also appears in the pre-gap JSON dependency merge e0727d73; the sample shows no new contributor taking over.
esri_geoportal-server.Notes: Geoportal Server v1 is explicitly retired, which makes its eight-month gap easier to explain. The two later changes update the README and website instead of restarting application development. Its July 2025 README commit still qualifies it as Active under the assignment's six-month rule, showing the limit of that rule.
esri_geoportal-server.reflection: The eight-month gap fits the repository's stated role as an archive. The [earlier README change](https://github.com/Esri/geoportal-server/commit/29a1c66ebfbcd8f44247fa73b96fed50f52aada1) already identifies v1 as retired. After the gap, [cd9bdd2f](https://github.com/Esri/geoportal-server/commit/cd9bdd2fbd4ffa07e3d7b50813c9ff462fc6af2b) keeps that warning and points readers to successor projects, while [3014a9ce](https://github.com/Esri/geoportal-server/commit/3014a9ce2120bd33ddde44bd4dae139775ec3785) changes the website text and badges. This is easier to interpret than an unexplained pause: the maintainers have documented the move away from v1. The return is limited documentation maintenance by an existing contributor. The required date rule can still label this repository Active, so that label should not be read as proof that v1 feature development has restarted.

microsoft_fhir-server.reflection: Every one of the 88 observed months has at least 3 dated commits. FHIR Server has substantial activity throughout 2020–2024, with annual totals between 2,776 and 3,369. Its low final point is a partial November 2025 month, and 12 undated records are omitted. hpparvi_pytransit.HypothesizedGapReason: Unknown. The last pre-gap commits handle CI, README text, and licensing; they do not explain the June–December 2015 pause. A mature-package maintenance pause is plausible, but no inspected source documents the cause.
hpparvi_pytransit.WhyRecovered: The first two January 2016 commits fix the z == k defect recorded in GitHub issue 12; numerical performance and release metadata work follow. This identifies the work that resumed activity, not a proven explanation of the preceding pause.
hpparvi_pytransit.WhoRecovered: Returning author Hannu Parviainen <hpparvi@gmail.com> wrote all first 10 post-gap commits; no new raw author identity appears in that window.
hpparvi_pytransit.Notes: The seven-month gap is difficult to explain because the pre-gap messages do not announce a stop. Activity resumes with fixes for the z == k bug in issue 12, followed by other numerical maintenance. The same author supplies all ten sampled recovery commits, and the dataset contains 967 dated commits after the gap.
hpparvi_pytransit.reflection: PyTransit has a seven-month author-time gap from June through December 2015. Before it, eight sampled commits concern CI, licensing, or merges, and two update documentation. Neither those messages nor the [historical README](https://github.com/hpparvi/PyTransit/blob/5470c458647cdbe0e4a4ebddd2dd21853bee2b72/README.md) explains why work stopped, so a routine maintenance pause remains only a hypothesis. Recovery is easier to interpret: [issue 12](https://github.com/hpparvi/PyTransit/issues/12), opened during the gap, reports failure when z equals k; [the first post-gap commit](https://github.com/hpparvi/PyTransit/commit/ba60c3080324344329fddbd0fbc114dd142465d9) fixes that case, with a follow-up the next day. Hannu Parviainen wrote all ten sampled recovery commits and already appears before the gap. Other and Bug fixes are the leading post-gap themes after the stated tie-break. The 967 later dated commits show substantial continuation, although they do not reveal the personal or organizational cause of the original pause.

sundmanbo_opencalphad.WhyRecovered: Commit bef99c4 and the June 18, 2024 changes.txt entry restart work on multicomponent MQMQA and Kohler–Toop extrapolations. October commits then concentrate on compilation, tests, and CI; the first ten post-gap commits span June through October rather than continuous monthly activity.
sundmanbo_opencalphad.WhoRecovered: Bo Sundman <bo.sundman@gmail.com> returns for the first two post-gap commits. The remaining eight are by zhongjingjogy <zhongjingjogy@gmail.com>, a raw identity absent from all dated pre-gap history.
sundmanbo_opencalphad.Notes: The five-month gap is consistent with the maintainer’s documented part-time development during retirement, although that does not prove the exact cause. Bo Sundman resumes model implementation in June 2024, and a new raw author identity later supplies build and CI work. Recovery is intermittent: the first ten post-gap commits extend into October.
sundmanbo_opencalphad.reflection: OpenCalphad has a five-month gap from January through May 2024 after model, XML-format, and bug-fix work. Its [historical change log](https://github.com/sundmanbo/opencalphad/blob/bef99c408b9a59e75a5f374a88c2fbecff0456b8/changes.txt) gives useful context: the maintainer described slow development and part-time work during retirement in 2023, then recorded renewed multicomponent MQMQA work in June 2024. Limited available time is therefore a reasonable hypothesis, but the log does not prove why each gap month was empty. Bo Sundman returns for two sampled commits; eight later commits come from the previously unseen raw identity zhongjingjogy and mostly address compilation, tests, and CI. This is intermittent recovery rather than an immediate steady stream. A [later comment about unsupported Python bindings](https://github.com/sundmanbo/opencalphad/issues/57#issuecomment-2395505367) also identifies competing tasks, but it was written in October and should not be treated as direct evidence of the earlier pause.

A May 29, 2024 question concerns the old Python interface; a same-day reply gives installation guidance, so issue discussion continued during the author-time gap.
On October 6, Bo Sundman says Python support is unavailable because of other tasks; evidence of competing priorities after, not a direct explanation of, the gap.
Diff changes the GEIN argument convention and model handling, clarifying the vague pre-gap message.
Diff separates XML routines into an included source file, supporting the XML development label.
Mixed routine reorganization, cleanup, and worked-example changes; supports a maintenance classification for this broad commit.

caveats: Maintainer time constraints are a hypothesis for the exact January–May gap, supported by nearby history rather than a statement naming those months.
First ten post-gap commits include a further lull between June and October.

stack-of-tasks_pinocchio.HypothesizedGapReason: Unknown brief pause. December 2014 is the only month in the longest zero run, shorter than the three-month threshold for counted inactivity gaps; inspected boundary messages and README do not identify a cause.
stack-of-tasks_pinocchio.WhyRecovered: The first January 2015 author-dated commits revise teaching labs for ISAE; subsequent commits handle upstream merges, build configuration, and initialization/constructor fixes. This is continuation of development, not evidence of a formally announced revival.
stack-of-tasks_pinocchio.WhoRecovered: All first-ten post-gap raw identities already occur before the gap: Mansard <nmansard@laas.fr> and Justin Carpentier using both <justin.carpentier@laas.fr> and <jcarpent@laas.fr>. No new raw identity appears in the sample.
stack-of-tasks_pinocchio.Notes: The longest zero run is only December 2014, so Pinocchio has no inactivity gap of at least three months. Returning contributors resume teaching-lab updates and routine development, but no inspected source explains the brief pause. The first selected commit has a January author date and March committer date, so the author-time plot is not an integration timeline.
stack-of-tasks_pinocchio.reflection: Pinocchio’s longest zero run is December 2014, only one month, and it has no gap meeting the three-month inactivity threshold. The pre-gap sample emphasizes robustness fixes and a lab robot model; the post-gap sample emphasizes routine maintenance and teaching documentation. The [first selected post-gap change](https://github.com/stack-of-tasks/pinocchio/commit/84c964d3285ce78a13b02c1a5745ed32ef42bd67) revises ISAE lab material, while the [boundary README](https://github.com/stack-of-tasks/pinocchio/blob/84c964d3285ce78a13b02c1a5745ed32ef42bd67/README.md) gives no explanation for the pause. Calling it abandonment would overstate this evidence. Mansard and both sampled Justin Carpentier identities already occur in pre-gap history. A timing caveat matters: the first commit’s author date is January 11, but its committer date is March 30, so author-time recovery is not necessarily the public integration date. The 11,320 later dated commits show extensive continuation, while the cause of that single empty month remains unknown.

agnwinds_python.WhyRecovered: June 2023 commits add radiation-hydrodynamics output columns and grid-generation scripts, followed by documentation and bug fixes. Preserved PR 1002 describes Knox’s rad-hydro work and has the exact merge SHA 74679f5 present in the post-gap sample.
agnwinds_python.WhoRecovered: Returning raw identities Knox S. Long <long@stsci.edu> and jhmatthews <matthews@ast.cam.ac.uk> supply the first ten post-gap commits; neither is new relative to all dated pre-gap history.
agnwinds_python.Notes: The two-month zero run is below the three-month inactivity threshold, and its cause is undocumented. Returning contributors resume radiation-hydrodynamics features, documentation, and fixes; preserved PR 1002 confirms the feature work. One missing timestamp could change the measured gap, and the later Sirocco rename should not be mistaken for its cause.
agnwinds_python.reflection: The agnwinds/python series has a two-month zero run in April–May 2023, shorter than the three-month inactivity threshold. Before it, the sample combines fixes, cleanup, and scattering or output features; afterward, features and documentation lead. [PR 998](https://github.com/sirocco-rt/sirocco/pull/998) preserves the pre-gap scattering work, and [PR 1002](https://github.com/sirocco-rt/sirocco/pull/1002) describes Knox’s radiation-hydrodynamics updates, matching the sampled June merge SHA. This supports continued research-driven development, but it does not explain why two months contain no dated commits. Knox S. Long and jhmatthews both appear before the gap, so the sampled recovery is by returning contributors. The [repository README](https://github.com/agnwinds/python/blob/main/README.md) explains the later October 2024 move to Sirocco; that change is not a cause of the 2023 gap. One commit lacks an author timestamp, so the measured empty run could change if its date becomes available.

csgillespie_powerlaw.HypothesizedGapReason: Unknown. The long December 2021–December 2023 author-time pause follows maintenance, CI setup, and a lognormal fix. A mature package receiving occasional maintenance is a plausible interpretation, but the inspected README and PR do not document a reason for the pause.
csgillespie_powerlaw.WhyRecovered: A January 2024 author-dated vignette-engine fix is followed in February 2025 by documentation tooling, pkgdown setup, and PR 103. Activity returns, but the 18 later dated commits and another long interval do not establish continuous recovery.
csgillespie_powerlaw.WhoRecovered: Colin Gillespie <csgillespie@gmail.com> returns. The only new raw string in the first-ten sample is csgillespie <csgillespie@gmail.com> on an automated gh-pages deployment; the matching email and inspected workflow give no evidence of a new human maintainer.
csgillespie_powerlaw.Notes: The 25-month gap has no documented cause in the inspected sources, and recovery looks like occasional package and documentation maintenance. A vignette fix is author-dated January 2024, but its PR is merged in February 2025, illustrating the difference between author time and integration time. The apparent new author string belongs to an automated site deployment using the existing maintainer’s email.
csgillespie_powerlaw.reflection: poweRlaw’s longest author-time gap spans December 2021 through December 2023, with eight zero runs of at least three months overall. Before the gap, maintenance and lognormal fixes dominate. The [boundary README](https://github.com/csgillespie/poweRlaw/blob/ad80bcd3ef7da449f65482e5a636718df874d88d/README.md) still presents an installable package, but it does not explain the pause. Occasional maintenance of a mature package is a plausible interpretation rather than a documented cause. Recovery concerns a vignette-engine fix and documentation tooling: [PR 103](https://github.com/csgillespie/poweRlaw/pull/103) was merged in February 2025 even though the first selected fix is author-dated January 2024. The 18 later dated commits therefore indicate a return of activity, not uninterrupted development. Colin Gillespie returns; the new raw author spelling on a generated site commit uses the same email, and the [deployment workflow](https://github.com/csgillespie/poweRlaw/blob/495efe6a481270830b703b52d55cc2a8bfad2dd0/.github/workflows/pkgdown.yaml) supports classifying it as automation rather than evidence of a new person.
